claims.text: Refractory HEAs such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30 or VFeTiTaW can be produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering.
These baseline refractory HEAs exhibit a multiphase microstructure containing bcc-type and Laves phases.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 2–5 at.% Cu to the refractory HEA.
Adding a small amount of Cu will enhance thermal conductivity relative to the Cu-free refractory HEA.
The Cu-modified alloy will preserve its multiphase structural integrity during high-temperature exposure and irradiation.
Annealing at approximately 1100–1500°C for about eight days is similar to conditions used in prior studies.
Ar+, He+, and D+ irradiation exposures are representative of the plasma-facing reactor intermediate-layer environment.
Added Cu atoms will either substitute into the refractory alloy lattice or segregate in a controlled manner at grain boundaries.
Cu substitution or controlled grain-boundary segregation will facilitate electron conduction.
Added Cu provides additional electron-conduction pathways that enhance lattice thermal conductivity.
The added Cu will not cause deleterious phase transformations or excessive segregation.
A 2–5 at.% Cu addition could produce greater than 10% improvement in thermal conductivity.
The Cu-modified alloy will retain mechanical properties similar to those of the baseline after annealing and irradiation.
Current Cu-free intermediate-layer refractory HEAs have lower electron-mediated heat-transfer capability than the proposed Cu-modified alloy.
The beneficial effect exists only over a narrow Cu concentration window, while excessive Cu can cause phase instability or harmful segregation.
Lattice thermal conductivity is a measurable response in a bulk Cu-containing HEA.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes enhancement of 'lattice thermal conductivity' to additional electron-conduction pathways. Electron-mediated thermal transport and lattice thermal conductivity are distinct transport contributions, so the stated mechanism does not consistently match the measured quantity.
